q: A site has a "Sign in with Google" button. Which one is it, and what comes back that OAuth alone does not give?
options: OAuth 2.0, and an access token that says who the user is
OpenID Connect, and an ID token that says who the user is
SAML, and a session cookie from Google
An API key from Google
why: OIDC is login built on top of OAuth. It adds the ID token. OAuth alone gives an app permission, not the user's identity.

q: A print shop app should read one user's files, but must never see her password. What do you use?
options: OAuth 2.0 with the authorization code flow and PKCE
Ask the user to paste her password into the app
SAML
A session cookie shared between both sites
why: OAuth gives the app a limited access token. The user logs in at the login server and says Allow, so her password never goes near the app.

q: An ID token has the right issuer and has not expired, but its `aud` is `other-app`. Your client id is `my-app`. What do you do?
options: Accept it, because the signature is valid
Accept it, because the issuer is right
Reject it, because the token was made for another app
Accept it but ask the user to confirm
why: A correctly signed token can still be meant for someone else. `aud` must contain your own client id, or an attacker can hand you a token from their app.

q: A build script calls your API at 3am. What is the simplest fit, and what do you store?
options: A session cookie, and you store the cookie
An API key with scopes, and you store only a hash of it
OIDC, and you store the ID token
SAML, and you store the XML
why: A key stands for a program with no person present. Store only a hash, so a database leak does not leak the keys, and let it carry scopes.

q: The login server accepts any redirect address that STARTS WITH the registered one. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, this is the safe way to match
An attacker can use an address like `/callback/evil` and steer the one-time code to themselves
It makes the login slower
It only matters for SAML
why: RFC 6749 says to compare redirect addresses with simple string comparison. Match exactly, including case and the query string.

q: A big customer's IT team says staff sign in with the company's own system and they only support SAML. What travels from their login system to your app?
options: A JSON ID token, sent straight from server to server
A signed XML assertion, carried through the browser
An API key
The staff member's password
why: In SAML the identity provider sends a signed XML assertion. The browser carries it to your app, so both sides must check signatures.
